2020-06: A church member appealed Presbytery’s affirmance of his conviction and excommunication for failing to heed Session admonition and membership vows, including prolonged absence from that church. The SJC affirmed and denied the appeal, holding that all four specifications—lack of reasonable indulgence, haste, prejudice, and injustice—were nonspecific and unsupported. It emphasized his admissions that the charges were true, the adequate timeline, and the bar on considering evidence not offered at trial. A dissent disputed his PCA membership, standing, and the Session’s jurisdiction.
2020-07: Pacific Presbytery allowed its Judicial Commission to read a six-page adverse report containing new assertions beyond TE Rankin Wilbourne's agreed BCO 38-1 confession, then ruled his sins "base and flagitious" and deposed him. The SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the deposition, holding BCO 38-1 barred the prejudicial report and BCO 34-7 did not apply without a pending trial. It recommended treating the 17-month censure as sufficient definite suspension, restoring ministerial standing without call, and closing the matter; dissolution of his call was not annulled.
2020-10: A complaint was filed with the SJC before Savannah River Presbytery completed its hearing on it. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order as prematurely filed and did not reach the merits. It reset the complainant's time to elevate the complaint so that timing begins on the later of notification of the SJC action or Presbytery's ruling. The SJC adopted the decision by roll call.
2020-11: The complaint against Southwest Florida Presbytery ended when the SJC approved Complainant David McWilliams's request to withdraw and abandon it, by unanimous roll-call vote (24-0-0) on March 25, 2021. The adopted decision recites no underlying dispute, merits analysis, or reasons and makes no substantive ruling; the complaint stands withdrawn and abandoned. The sparse record is useful only as an example of an approved pre-decision withdrawal/abandonment.
2020-12: Ryan Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its refusal to commence process against Greg Johnson on four allegations concerning same-sex attraction as sin, identity in Christ, sanctification, and fitness for office. The SJC denied the complaint in full. It found no clear procedural error and held that Johnson’s explanations and clarifications made Presbytery’s non-indictment judgments reasonable. No trial was ordered. The ruling neither adjudged Johnson guilty nor endorsed every statement or broader constitutional position concerning same-sex attraction.
2020-13: The SJC dismissed Peter Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery as administratively out of order because he lacked standing to complain of the Presbytery's action. Benyola was neither a teaching elder member of that Presbytery nor a ruling elder commissioner representing a member church at the September 18, 2020 meeting when the Presbytery considered and denied the complaint. Citing prior SJC standing decisions, the Commission held the defect could not be cured and dismissed unanimously, 22-0-0, without reaching the merits.
2020-14: At a meeting of the Session of Providence Presbyterian Church (PPC), Edwardsville, Illinois, following a history of difficulties in the marriage of Danielle Myers (Mrs. Myers) and TE Aaron Myers (TE Myers) spanning at least two years, TE Myers was asked to resign from his pastoral charge. He complied. Six of the ruling elders of Providence Presbyterian Church wrote to the Stated Clerk of Illiana Presbytery bringing a recommendation of charges against TE Myers with respect to his treatment of Mrs. Myers.
2021-01: The SJC held that Stuart Michelson's complaint against Northwest Georgia Presbytery was administratively out of order because he filed it with the SJC before Presbytery had completed its hearing on the complaint. The SJC did not reach the merits. It reset Michelson's time to elevate the complaint to run from the later of notification of the SJC's action or Presbytery's ruling on the complaint. Approved 22-0-0.
2021-02: In this BCO 40-5 request, the SJC advised the Stated Clerk that Tippins v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery should be referred to the General Assembly's Review of Presbytery Records Committee. The SJC approved that action 19-3-0; three commissioners dissented. The sparse record supplies no underlying facts, merits analysis, or reason for the referral.
2021-03: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.
2021-05: The SJC held an October 2021 complaint against Southwest Florida Presbytery administratively out of order because the complainants had affiliated with another branch of the visible church on February 9, 2020, ending PCA jurisdiction over them under BCO 38-3. They therefore lacked standing. The ruling reached no merits and supplies no description of the underlying presbytery action; the vote was 22-0-0, with Lucas and White absent.
2021-06: Herron and others challenged Presbytery’s decision to proceed to trial after a BCO 31-2 finding, his administrative suspension, denial of access to Presbytery records and meetings, and a public statement. The SJC sustained only the access issue: suspension from official functions did not remove his membership rights, though it did not entitle him to every investigative-committee document. Finding no clear error on the other issues, it ordered trial to proceed, temporarily stayed censure decisions, and postponed related complaints through trial and any appeal.
2021-07: RE Acree attempted to complain directly to Tennessee Valley Presbytery about action taken at a meeting where he was not a commissioner. The SJC found the complaint administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order because BCO 43-1 gave him no standing to complain against that action. It added that Presbytery should itself have declined to adjudicate the complaint.
2021-08: As of March 3, 2022, Presbytery had not supplied formally adopted responses to records-review exceptions, although its clerk had prepared drafts. The SJC allowed time for adoption and filing by April 1, after which it would forward the responses for records review; failure to file would prompt a called hearing. This was an unfinished compliance process, not approval of the draft responses or a final merits decision.
2021-09: 12/30/19 Grace and Peace PCA purchased Prince of Peace Lutheran Church. 01/02/20 Mr. Miller emailed TE Lee Veazey, pastor of Grace and Peace, requesting that certain things be removed from the church building. Below are some excerpts.
2021-10: 09/25/18 TE F. Todd Williams was indicted by the Chesapeake Presbytery Judicial Commission (CPJC) and charged with "failure to maintain his own family well... and to walk with exemplary piety before the flock... of God." Three specifications were formulated in the indictment. 11/13/18 TE Williams confessed to some of the sins outlined in the indictment and requested that the matter be treated as a BCO 38- 1 Case Without Process.
2021-11: Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s action because discipline preceded particular charges and a specific confession, and because an independent church lacked authority to impose PCA censure. It declared the underlying matter moot because the alleged event was twenty-one years old and the victim would not cooperate, ending the proceeding without remand. The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically.
2021-12: The Michelsons’ complaint challenged a congregational meeting’s procedure for electing three assistant pastors as associate pastors—allegedly without a pulpit committee, ballots, counted abstentions, or protection for a substantial minority. The SJC dismissed it as not judicially in order: BCO 43-1 requires complaint against an act or decision of a court, but the complaint attacked congregational actions, while the Session’s only act was calling the meeting and was not objected to. The SJC noted other possible redress; the dissent found the Session’s call and recommendation justiciable.
2021-13: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.
2021-14: Herron challenged Presbytery's handling of its directive that he withdraw his civil defamation lawsuit. The SJC answered the complaint by reference to its completed trial decision in 2022-10, which acquitted him on all seven charges, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to ministerial good standing. The incorporated decision found the lawsuit's sinfulness unproved; the complaint notice supplied no separate issue-by-issue ruling.
2021-15: Barber and others challenged Presbytery's actions rescinding Herron's contumacy judgment. The SJC answered their complaint by reference to its completed trial decision in 2022-10, which acquitted Herron on all seven charges, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to ministerial good standing. That decision found the lawsuit's sinfulness unproved, undermining the related contumacy charge. The complaint notice supplied no separate issue-by-issue ruling.
2022-01: The SJC dismissed Eric Eagle and others' complaint against Savannah River Presbytery as administratively out of order and untimely under BCO 43-3. The complaint was first filed prematurely in December 2020; after the SJC reset the filing clock to the later of its October 21, 2021 action or Presbytery's October 20, 2020 ruling, it was filed more than 30 days later. The merits were not reached. An attached SJC response to CCB separately defended its record-reopening in Case 2020-12 and asked CCB to deny an exception request as untimely, waived, and procedural.
2022-02: The SJC answered this Herron-related complaint by reference to its final decision in the Herron trial, which acquitted him on all seven charges, removed all censures and administrative suspensions imposed by Presbytery, and restored his good standing as a minister. The complaint notice supplies no separate ruling on its individual allegations.
2022-03: Philadelphia Presbytery declared that TE Larry Smith's views on continuing prophecy and tongues were not out of accord or hostile to the system of doctrine. Klett et al. complained. The SJC sustained the complaint: Smith's written views affirmed continuing non-general revelation and treated prophecy and tongues as public-worship elements, contrary to WCF 1 and 21, so Presbytery erred under BCO 21-4.f. The SJC annulled Presbytery's May 15, 2021 action. No further action was possible because Smith and his congregation had left the PCA; the matter was concluded, with precedent limited to the written views reviewed.
2022-04: The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.
2022-05: Three Ruling Elders complained of errors in judicial process against them. The SJC found the complaint out of order and moot because the Session had dismissed every charge and ended the process, while the elders had voluntarily resigned and requested dissolution of their calls. Because these events removed the challenged action and settled the underlying dispute, the SJC did not reach the alleged procedural errors.
2022-07: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.
2022-08: The SJC held that RE David Snoke's complaint against Pittsburgh Presbytery's January 29, 2022 action was administratively out of order and could not be put in order because Snoke, not a commissioner from his church to that meeting, lacked standing to complain. Although Presbytery later voted 20-16-3 to find the complaint in order, the SJC said it should have been ruled out of order. The SJC did not reach the merits. Its vote was 20-1, with three absent.
2022-09: The SJC declared Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order, because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The decision was adopted 23-0 on a roll call, one absent, on the officers' recommendation. The record does not identify the underlying presbytery action or reach the complaint's merits, so the case's value is its threshold standing ruling, not any complaint determination.
2022-10: On a BCO 41 reference, the SJC tried a minister on seven charges arising from allegations of sexual misconduct, bullying, dishonesty, a civil defamation suit, contumacy, doctrinal error, and lack of fitness. It found him not guilty on every charge because the prosecution failed to meet its burden, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to good standing. For the lawsuit charge, it rejected a categorical ban on civil suits between Christians and required proof that this suit was sinful.
2022-11: The SJC had postponed BCO 34-1 petitions concerning Central Indiana Presbytery until the Herron trial concluded. After acquitting Herron on all charges and restoring him to good standing, the SJC answered and decided the petitions by reference to that final trial decision. The petitions were thus resolved through incorporation of the trial result, not transferred to another court; the trial itself arose from a distinct BCO 41 reference.
2022-12: The SJC dismissed two BCO 34-1 overtures asking the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction over alleged doctrinal errors by TE Greg Johnson. After Memorial Presbyterian Church withdrew from the PCA and Missouri Presbytery removed Johnson's name from its rolls under BCO 38-3a, the SJC held it lacked authority to assume original jurisdiction because the PCA no longer had jurisdiction over him. The dismissal did not resolve the doctrinal allegations; one commissioner dissented.
2022-13: Wade Miller challenged his Session’s May 19, 2021 letter standing by its decision to permit a non-church yoga class to meet on church property. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order: that letter triggered BCO 43-1’s 60-day deadline, but Miller filed with the Session on November 20, 2021, and no new Session action occurred within the preceding 60 days. Citing a one-day-late precedent, the SJC reached no merits.
2022-14: The SJC dismissed Oh’s complaint against Korean Southeast Presbytery following his withdrawal of it. The brief decision does not identify the challenged presbytery action, address the merits, or grant substantive relief.
2022-15: A complaint against South Florida Presbytery was held administratively out of order because its sole complainant died on November 15, 2022, and no other person joined the original complaint. The SJC adopted that disposition by a 23–0 roll-call vote. The sparse record states no underlying complaint issue, merits analysis, or further proceedings; the ruling turns on the absence of a surviving or joined complainant.
2022-16: The SJC declined to reach a complaint arising from judicial process against three ruling elders (not the complainants), because the Session dismissed all charges and ended that process on July 23, 2022, and the elders resigned and their calls were dissolved. The SJC found the complaint out of order and moot, with no merits ruling, and approved the decision 23-0. The case illustrates that termination of the underlying judicial process and voluntary resignations can moot a complaint about that process.
2022-17: Standing to complain: The SJC found three complaints by Peter Benyola against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The SJC approved the ruling 23-0 on March 2, 2023; the supplied record does not describe the underlying allegations.
2022-20: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.
2022-21: A minister challenged Presbytery’s procedures and its classification of a transfer candidate’s views on continuing tongues as “not a difference.” The SJC rejected the procedural objections because Presbytery could disregard its committee’s recommendation and had breached no required procedure. It nevertheless held that a difference need not overtly contradict the Standards and that the candidate’s statements implicated WCF 1.1 and 1.6. It annulled the classification and remanded for clarification and a new judgment, without deciding whether the clarified view would be acceptable.
2022-22: Presbytery investigated a Session's handling of sexual-misconduct allegations and found it guilty of delinquencies without a trial. The SJC upheld Presbytery's authority to receive credible reports and investigate, but annulled the findings of guilt, censures, and corrective mandates because BCO 40-6 required formal process or an admission before censure. It returned the matter for records review, informal resolution, or formal process and declined interim mandates that would assume the disputed allegations were true.
2022-23: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.
2023-01: Kristin Hann's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery was dismissed because the SJC held she lacked standing: she was not subject to Pee Dee Presbytery's jurisdiction, so the complaint was judicially out of order and could not be put in order. The SJC made no merits ruling and stated that the ruling did not stay Presbytery's continuing investigation or review of resulting actions. The adopted ruling was approved 17-2; Maynard and Sartorius dissented without stated reasons, four were absent, and Ross recused.
2023-02: The SJC dismissed Mrs. Kappie Reynolds's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery as judicially out of order. The complaint challenged a Session's reception of and action on a confession at a meeting more than six months before filing, far outside BCO 43-2's sixty-day period; the SJC held the untimeliness was not demonstrated curable. The ruling expressly reserved whether Reynolds could proceed as an injured party under BCO 31-5 and whether the Session had jurisdiction over claims outside the received confession.
2023-04: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.
2023-05: Former church employee Emily Hyland complained to the SJC after Chicago Metro Presbytery ruled her BCO 43 complaint out of order because, as a local-church member, she was not subject to Presbytery's jurisdiction. The SJC was equally divided 12–12–0 on the proposed panel decision, so CMP's ruling stands. That proposed decision would have answered that CMP did not err: Hyland lacked standing to file a BCO 43-1 complaint with Presbytery. No amendments were made. An evenly divided SJC thus leaves the lower ruling in place without a majority rationale.
2023-06: Session elders challenged Presbytery’s handling of a mediation complaint, investigative directives, BCO 40-5 reports, and a trial stay. The SJC held that the mediation complaint was never formally filed and became moot; official-record requests were proper, but compelling nonrecord personal communications and requiring the Session to address its congregation exceeded Presbytery’s authority. It vacated the communications directive and annulled the stay for lack of the required prior citation. It upheld committee examination of the BCO 40-5 reports and did not reach alleged partiality; the Session trials were to proceed.
2023-07: Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the divestiture because BCO 38-3(a) had already ended Presbytery's jurisdiction while he was in good standing and under no investigation or charges. It directed Presbytery to record the irregular withdrawal, acknowledge his new membership, and remove him from its roll.
2023-09: An elder appealed Presbytery’s elevation, without additional process, of suspensions from office and the Sacraments to deposition and excommunication. The SJC granted the appeal, reversed in whole, and remanded, restoring the prior suspensions. Elevation required a hearing on incorrigibility and contumacy—with a charge, evidence, plea, and defense—but not a full de novo trial; disagreement with the original verdict alone was insufficient. The SJC left unresolved deposition from office when excommunication is absent.
2023-10: Elders challenged Presbytery’s authority and vague instruction for its Shepherding Committee to “follow up” with their Session. The SJC denied the constitutional challenge because the record reasonably supported concern for the church’s peace and spiritual welfare, but sustained the challenge to Presbytery’s lack of specific direction and poor communication. The decision distinguishes prohibited mandatory visitation without cause from a reasonably justified visit, while requiring clarity about its objectives. It did not decide the underlying doxology dispute or order further relief.
2023-11: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.
2023-13: A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery's failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord's Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church's session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly's direct referral but did not void it.
2023-14: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.
2023-15: Turner complained against Presbytery Judicial Commission actions deposing TE Tommy Boland and dissolving Cross Community Church’s relationship with Presbytery. The SJC ruled both complaints administratively out of order for lack of standing and incapable of being put in order. Cross Community had already disaffiliated through its first congregational motion; the second motion, which contemplated later implementation, was out of order as contingent. Because no Presbytery action was required to effect disaffiliation, Turner was no longer a PCA member. The underlying challenges were not decided.
2023-16: 10/25/22 SJC ruled in case 2022-04 that HP erred in both matters brought before it by Arden Presbyterian Church's ("APC") previous pastor, stating, "Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting any of the allegations embraced by the subject matter of this case." 11/13/22 RE Brett Callaway wrote the APC Session expressing concern over an APC Session proposal to send a letter to the Highlands Presbytery to “affirm the Christian character of Kevin, Jill, and Delaney Martin."
2023-18: 2019 TE John Barrett, of another PCA Presbytery, contacted TE Richard Schwartz, a member of NP's Shepherding Committee (“SC”), with allegations of sin against TE Sears, dating from 2010 and 2011 and involving Ms. W, who by then had become a member of the congregation that TE Barrett served as a Pastor.
2023-19: A filing challenging Presbytery’s handling of Huffman’s BCO 38-1 confession was styled as an appeal under a newly amended rule. The SJC found it judicially out of order because the case began and was nearly completed when the former rule provided review by complaint, and retroactive application would be unfair. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the filing as a complaint at its next stated meeting; denial or failure to act permits review by the SJC. No merits issue was decided.
2023-20: 07/11/22 Stated meeting of the Session of Valley Presbyterian Church (hereafter "VPC") at which by vote of 5-3, the Session, approved a motion "to have God's blessings as formal benedictions to conclude the service and not doxologies." 08/09/22 Session members RE Riedinger and Shaw and filed a timely BCO 43-1 Complaint with the Session regarding that decision.[^fn-ga52-p885-n15]
2023-21: 06/02/22 The SJC issued its decision in Case No. 2021-11 sustaining the Complaint and determining that further action was moot because the primary alleged victim of the offense declined to participate in Presbytery's investigation or actions regarding the Accused.
2024-01: The Session of Walnut Hill Presbyterian Church (WHPC) had discussions with TE Andy Moehn (pastor of WHPC) regarding his concerns about the state of his marriage. Equine couples therapy was begun. The Session of WHPC met with TE and Mrs. Moehn to discuss the state of their marriage and correspondence each had sent to Session. The ruling elders of WHPC had several other meetings in February to consider the state of the marriage.
2024-18: 2020 The Church transferred from the Reformed Church in America into the PCA.
2025-12: Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s divestiture of their offices after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC reversed because their calls had never been formally dissolved, so they were not automatically without call, and BCO 34-10 did not apply while they remained actively engaged and accepted in ministry. The SJC could not judge their fairness and pretext claims from the record. It restored them to good standing and required Presbytery to dissolve the existing calls before pursuing lawful alternatives.
